question:
Patient note:
A 63-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department by her adult daughter after she experienced two bouts of coffee-ground–colored vomiting at home earlier this morning, the larger of which filled roughly half of a cereal bowl; she reported an acrid metallic taste in her mouth but was able to walk to the car without feeling faint, never losing consciousness, and never requiring assistance to remain upright. Her last bowel movement had occurred the preceding evening and was described as medium brown, soft, and without the sticky tar or foul odor sometimes associated with digested blood. Over the prior week she had noticed a dull, burning pressure beneath the xiphoid that flared after the evening meal and occasionally radiated toward the left costal margin; the discomfort was partially relieved by chewing calcium carbonate tablets and had not awakened her from sleep. She denied dizziness, blackout spells, chest pain, shortness of breath when lying flat, ankle swelling, or needing extra pillows at night, and she could climb the flight of stairs to her second-floor apartment at her usual pace. Her medical history is notable for a chronic viral liver infection diagnosed in her late thirties that led to compensated stage-3 fibrosis confirmed on a transient elastography two years ago; she remains under hepatology follow-up every six months and takes ledipasvir/sofosbuvir, which achieved an undetectable viral load last year, along with vitamin D supplementation. She has never been hospitalized for fluid retention, jaundice, encephalopathy, or gastrointestinal variceal bleeding, and her most recent abdominal ultrasound showed a normal portal vein diameter without ascites. Additional diagnoses include well-controlled type 2 diabetes managed with metformin 850 mg twice daily, osteoarthritis of both knees for which she intermittently takes over-the-counter naproxen 220 mg twice a day, and mild gastroesophageal reflux that prompted her primary care physician to start omeprazole 20 mg each morning six months ago; she admits to missing several doses of the proton-pump inhibitor this month because of out-of-town travel. She does not take aspirin, antiplatelet agents, anticoagulants, or herbal supplements. Surgical history is limited to laparoscopic cholecystectomy at age 45. She quit smoking cigarettes fifteen years ago after a twenty-pack-year habit and now drinks a glass of wine only on special occasions; she has never used recreational drugs. Her father died from myocardial infarction at 72, and her mother had rheumatoid arthritis. Upon arrival, before any intravenous access was established, triage documented a blood pressure of 121/74 mm Hg measured manually in the seated position, a regular pulse of 86 beats per minute, respiratory rate 17 breaths per minute, oral temperature 37.1 °C, and oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air. She appeared mildly anxious but was speaking in full sentences, skin warm and dry, and capillary refill under two seconds. Conjunctival pallor was subtle but present; sclerae were anicteric, and there were no spider angiomata or palmar erythema noted on inspection of the upper torso. Jugular venous pulsation was not visible with the head of the bed at 30°, heart sounds were crisp with a normal S1 and S2 and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and lungs were clear throughout. The abdomen was flat and soft with mild tenderness in the epigastrium on deep palpation, no rebound or guarding, a liver edge palpable 1 cm below the costal margin but smooth and non-tender, and no splenomegaly or ascites was appreciated. Bowel sounds were present and normoactive. No lower-extremity edema was observed. Neurologic screening revealed an alert, oriented patient with intact cranial nerves and normal motor strength. A rectal examination produced a small amount of brown stool that turned the guaiac card faintly blue after several seconds but showed no visible dark tar. Venous blood specimens drawn prior to any fluid resuscitation, acid suppression, or antiemetic therapy demonstrated hemoglobin 12.0 g/dL, hematocrit 36 %, mean corpuscular volume 89 fL, platelet count 198 × 10³/µL, white blood cell count 7.6 × 10³/µL, blood urea nitrogen 15 mg/dL, serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 104 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, glucose 118 mg/dL, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, albumin 3.9 g/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 48 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 52 U/L, and an international normalized ratio of 1.1. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained simultaneously revealed normal sinus rhythm at 87 beats per minute without ischemic changes. Upright chest radiography showed clear lung fields and an unremarkable cardiac silhouette, and abdominal radiograph depicted nonspecific bowel gas without free air. Two peripheral 18-gauge cannulas were placed after labs were sent, a type and screen was ordered, and the patient was kept NPO while awaiting evaluation by the gastroenterology service for further management of her suspected upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score uses admission BUN, sex-specific hemoglobin, systolic BP, pulse, melena, syncope, hepatic disease, and heart failure.
BUN 15 mg/dL is below the first scoring threshold (about 18.2 mg/dL): 0. Hemoglobin 12.0 g/dL is at the female zero-point cutoff (≥12.0): 0. Systolic BP 121 mm Hg (≥110): 0. Pulse 86/min (<100): 0.
Melena: 0; the stool was brown, and a positive guaiac test is not melena. Syncope: 0. Hepatic disease: +2 for chronic viral liver disease with stage-3 fibrosis, even though it is compensated. Heart failure: 0. Coffee-ground emesis itself does not add points.
Total = 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 2.
Final answer: 2
